claims.text: The baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy is equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
Increasing the relative Hf percentage in HfNbTaTiZr systematically increases mechanical strength.
Increasing the relative Hf percentage in HfNbTaTiZr systematically increases hardness.
The proposed increases in strength and hardness arise from enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
Changing Hf concentration induces local variations in lattice distortion.
Changing Hf concentration alters atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Increasing Hf concentration produces greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Enhanced solid-solution strengthening improves yield strength and hardness.
A combinatorial compositionally graded sample or library can be used to study the effects of changing elemental percentages.
The compositionally graded approach can maintain a consistent processing history across the investigated composition range.
Elevated-Hf samples will have greater hardness than the baseline alloy.
Elevated-Hf samples will have greater yield strength than the baseline alloy.
Hardness and yield strength will increase monotonically with Hf percentage over the studied composition range.
Extreme compositions or high-temperature conditions may not follow the predicted trend.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property change may depend on interactions among constituents, grain size, and processing variables.
Composition mapping combined with high-throughput nanoindentation can test the relationship between local Hf concentration and hardness.
